title: Bhangani in his words
hook: he describes the battle of Bhangani in vivid verse (Bachitar Natak 8)
tomorrow: He gave his head, not his faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't call me God: the tenth Guru names himself the servant, come to see the play of the world. Your line was only the servant. Who did you pass the credit to? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

War stories usually reach us secondhand. A historian's summary, a movie, an uncle who heard it from someone. Rarely does the person at the center pick up a pen and tell it, beat by beat, in verse. In Bachitar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh does that for a battle fought at a place called Bhangani. He names the men who stood with him. He writes the noise. He doesn't hide that arrows came at him too.
screen: `WAR STORIES, SECONDHAND.` → `THE GURU PICKS UP THE PEN.` → `A BATTLE AT BHANGANI.`

segments.voice: Here is the outline of his account, in paraphrase. Fateh Shah, a hill king, comes against him, and the Guru writes that he came without cause. The two sides meet. And then the verse changes speed. The meters quicken, the lines clatter like hooves, and the poem names people. His kinsman Sango Shah fights hard and falls. His uncle Kirpal goes into the fight with a heavy club, and the Guru describes him like a warrior from the old epics. A chief on the other side, Hari Chand, looses arrows, and the Guru writes that one reached him, and that he answered with arrows of his own. In the end the hill forces break, and the Guru gives the victory to the grace of the Timeless One. So what is this doing in a book Sikhs hold sacred? Three things. First, honesty. He doesn't paint himself as untouchable. He was hit. Kinsmen died. The cost is in the poem. Second, honor for others. Kinsmen and companions are named, so they're remembered. The Guru's story is crowded with people. Third, the frame from two days ago. This is a scene in the wondrous drama, and its hero isn't him. He came through, he says, because the One carried him through. Sikh tradition remembers Bhangani as a battle the Guru didn't seek and fought to defend his people. You don't have to love battle poetry to take something from it. A hard day, told truthfully, names the cost, names who stood with you, and gives thanks for getting to the other side.
screen: `A HILL KING COMES WITHOUT CAUSE.` · `THE VERSE QUICKENS; MEN ARE NAMED.` · `HE WAS HIT; HE ANSWERED.` · `THE COST, THE COMPANIONS, THE GRACE.` · then, large: `THROUGH THE BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall a hard day you came through. Settle, and breathe. Choose one day that was a battle in its own way: a diagnosis, a layoff, a fight with someone you love, a long night in a waiting room. Tell it to yourself the way the Guru tells Bhangani. What did it cost? Who stood with you? Name them, one by one. Then notice that you're here, on the other side of it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru with thanks on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhangani in his words. The tenth Guru's own verse account of a battle: honest about the cost, generous to those beside him, grateful to the One who carried him through. Today's word.
Your line: through the battle. Today, thank one person who stood with you on a hard day, by name. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.
